read.passage: Every day, millions of images and stories go viral before anyone has checked whether they are true. Fact-checkers argue that the problem is not a lack of information but a lack of patience. Rarely do people stop to ask who created a post, or why. Yet a few simple habits can make a real difference. First, look for the original source: a claim that cannot be traced back to a named person or organisation should be treated with caution. Second, cross-check the story with at least two reliable news outlets. Third, notice your own emotions. Posts designed to make us angry or afraid are, by and large, the ones most likely to be misleading. None of this requires special training; it simply requires us to pause before we press 'share'.

qs.q: According to fact-checkers, what is the main problem?

read2.passage: It is often claimed that humans use only ten percent of their brains. The idea has been repeated in films, advertisements and self-help books, yet neuroscientists dismiss it outright. Brain scans show that virtually every region is active over the course of a day, and even simple tasks draw on networks spread across the whole brain. So why does the myth persist? Partly, it seems, because it is flattering: if most of our brain lies unused, we must all have hidden potential waiting to be unlocked. Psychologists also note that the claim has no clear origin, which makes it hard to disprove for anyone who does not check the original research. The lesson, researchers argue, extends well beyond the brain: the more appealing a claim is, the more carefully it deserves to be examined.

options: Simple tasks use one small region.
Nearly every region is active during a day.
Only ten percent of the brain is used.
